analysis.one_liner: Allows automated and prerecorded 'informational' calls to cell phones and overrides state robocall rules.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Committee, held one subcommittee hearing in November 2011, and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal robocall law (the TCPA) so that companies could use autodialers and prerecorded voices to call cell phones for any commercial purpose that is not a sales pitch — things like account notices, collections calls, and other 'informational' calls. It would have narrowed the definition of the equipment counts as an autodialer, treated anyone who gives a company their phone number as having agreed to be called, and blocked states from enforcing stricter robocall rules on anything except telemarketing calls. The bill never got a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that place large volumes of automated calls — banks, debt collectors, utilities, and other service businesses — would be able to autodial and play recorded messages to cell phones without getting prior consent, as long as the call is not a sales solicitation. This would cut their costs and expand their reach, since the current law generally bans autodialed calls to cell numbers without consent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, debt collectors, and automated callers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let automated or prerecorded calls be made to any cell phone or any service where the called party pays for the call, so long as the call is for a commercial purpose that is not a telephone solicitation [S3].

It would define 'prior express consent' so that a person who provides a phone number as a contact automatically consents to calls from any business they have a relationship with — consent given at purchase or any other point in the relationship [S2][S3].
It would narrow the legal definition of an 'automatic telephone dialing system' to equipment that generates random or sequential numbers, excluding many modern dialing tools from the ban [S3].
It would bar states from imposing any requirement on calls regulated under the section, except for telephone solicitations, wiping out state robocall protections for non-solicitation calls [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cell phone users would bear the cost: unwanted automated calls to numbers where the receiver pays for the call, minutes used on calls people did not agree to, and the loss of the ability to sue or rely on state rules for non-telemarketing robocalls.

drawbacks.text: Consumers would pay for calls they never agreed to: the bill explicitly permits autodialed calls to any service 'for which the called party is charged for the call' when the call is not a solicitation [S3].
Providing a phone number anywhere in a business relationship would count as consent to automated calls, eliminating the current requirement of actual prior approval [S2][S3].
States could no longer enforce their own robocall restrictions on anything except telemarketing calls, overriding stronger state consumer protections [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to high-volume callers, who would gain a legal path to autodial cell phones without consent and avoid litigation under the existing robocall ban. The costs fall on cell phone users, who would pay for and receive more unwanted automated calls and lose state-level protections. On balance this is a transfer of convenience and legal protection from consumers to commercial callers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in November 2011, and died there without ever being brought to the full House for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lee Terry (R-NE), joined by Rep. Edolphus Towns (D-NY), introduced the bill on September 22, 2011 [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on November 4, 2011, but the full committee never acted and the House never voted on the bill before the 112th Congress ended [S5].
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, 9 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cell phone users are better off because the bill died: the existing ban on autodialed and prerecorded calls to cell phones without consent remains in force, along with state robocall protections. Commercial callers did not get the exemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cell phone users, not automated callers

for.name: Rep. Lee Terry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow informational autodialed calls to cell phones.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Joined the sponsor at introduction as the bill's Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 22, 2011 and never reported the bill out; it died in the committee and its subcommittee after a single hearing.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship leaned heavily Republican (9 of 10 cosponsors were Republicans), though the sponsor recruited one senior Democrat as an original cosponsor; no floor vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Telemarketing and automated calling firms (debt collectors, banks, utilities, service businesses)
industries.note: The bill would have let these callers autodial cell phones without prior consent for any non-solicitation commercial purpose and would have narrowed the equipment definition and preempted state rules. Because it died, the existing ban on autodialed cell calls without consent stayed in place.

industries.industry: Consumers with paid-per-minute or prepaid cell service
industries.note: The bill's failure preserved the ban on calls to services where the recipient pays for the call, sparing these users charges for unwanted automated calls.
